items.title: 🔓 [Macworld] U.K. government ordered to reveal secret Apple backdoor demand
items.content_html:
Macworld

The U.K.’s Investigatory Powers Tribunal today ruled that the British government must confirm that it demanded access to Apple customers’ data in 2025.

Early last year, the Washington Post was tipped off about the secret order, or “technical capability notice,” which ordered Apple to “create a back door allowing [U.K. authorities] to retrieve all the content any Apple user worldwide has uploaded to the cloud.” At the time, we warned that such an order would instantly compromise the security of more than two billion Apple users across the globe.

Apple resisted, choosing to remove the ADP feature from U.K. iPhones rather than comply with the order, and it was subsequently reported that British politicians had given up on the scheme. But while it was common knowledge that the attempt had been made, the Home Office refused to acknowledge this, arguing that revealing the existence of the order would damage national security and the public interest.

Apple itself was not permitted to disclose that it had received a technical capability notice. Until now the company has adhered to this even while commenting in carefully non-specific terms on the situation. At one point, for example, it stated that “we have never built a backdoor or master key to any of our products, and we never will” without actually confirming it had been ordered to do so in this case.

But now, finally, as TechCrunch reports, the national security argument has been put to rest.

Having noted that “anyone with even a passing interest in this topic already knows that the respondent has served a technical capability notice on Apple,” the three judges indicate that they “reject the respondent’s contention that it would be damaging to national security to confirm the fact that the respondent has given Apple a technical capability notice.”

It should be noted that this judgment refers to the existence of the order rather than its specific details. The judges say this is “another matter” which “is better addressed separately.” The case, in other words, is not finished yet.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] Anthropic’s IPO filing reveals a strategy to undercut its AI rivals
items.content_html:
Welcome to AI Decoded, Fast Company‘s weekly newsletter that breaks down the most important news in the world of AI. I’m Mark Sullivan, a senior writer at Fast Company, covering emerging tech, AI, and tech policy.

Sign up to receive this newsletter every week via email here. And if you have comments on this issue and/or ideas for future ones, drop me a line at sullivan@fastcompany.com, and follow me on X @thesullivan.

‘Compute multipliers’ and ‘Anthropic Direct’ may be the IPO’s secret sauce

As frontier models from Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google converge in capabilities, the companies selling them may end up competing for enterprise business less on model quality and more on the cost of the computing power needed to run them. In its IPO filing and investor roadshow video, Anthropic, which debuted on the Nasdaq on Thursday, suggested it may be preparing for that future with something called “compute multipliers” and a compute-sourcing model it calls Anthropic Direct.

In its S-1, filed publicly in October, Anthropic defines compute multipliers as “algorithmic and methodological” improvements in the way it trains and operates models, effectively increasing the computing power it can get from a given amount of capacity. And these multipliers are “stackable.” In its roadshow video, Anthropic says it measures “total effective compute,” which is its physical computing capacity multiplied by the multipliers it has discovered or expects to discover in the future. Its example: If a model takes 100 units of compute to train, a 4x multiplier lets Anthropic train the same model with 25 units, or use all 100 units to train a model that would previously have required 400.

The company also says the multipliers “stack,” with each new discovery building on previous ones, and that it expects Claude will eventually be able to discover multipliers on its own.

According to the filing, the gains apply to models used to serve customers as well as to model training. Anthropic says its researchers “have delivered meaningful compute multipliers for inference,” reducing the computing power needed to deliver a given level of model performance. The company says this “allows us to provide greater value for customers.”

Anthropic has already been cutting prices. It says price reductions tied to new model versions, along with contractual discounts, reduced revenue growth by about $600 million between the second and third quarters of 2026. It says Opus 5.5, launched in September, delivered “a lower cost per task” than earlier models. If Anthropic can get more usable compute out of each chip than its rivals can, it may be able to undercut other AI labs on price. It may also be able to undercut cloud providers that sell AI services built on their own models.

If compute multipliers let Anthropic do more with its physical computing power, Anthropic Direct could give the company greater control over where that power comes from. Right now, Anthropic buys almost all its computing power from cloud providers, including competitors like SpaceX, Amazon Web Services, Microsoft, and CoreWeave. The company says it has already committed to buying roughly $900.9 billion in compute from these providers over the coming years and decades. Those expenses also include short-term cloud compute purchases, mainly to cover peak usage periods, which come at a premium.

The S-1 says Anthropic is reducing its reliance on expensive cloud providers by developing its own data centers and leasing the chips that go inside them. Its first Anthropic Direct facility came online this year. The company says a “significant portion” of its planned compute spending will go toward building more Anthropic Direct capacity. Based on an analysis of contract values in the S-1 filing, PitchBook estimates that Direct data centers will supply about 1% of Anthropic’s available compute capacity this year, 48% in 2030, and 60% in 2035.

The S-1 says Anthropic’s total compute pool, including third-party cloud compute and Direct, will be used for its own research and model development, as well as customer workloads. Bringing more compute in-house could dramatically reduce the overhead costs of developing and serving Claude models, apps, and agents for enterprise and consumer customers. That, in turn, could allow Anthropic to lower per-token prices for enterprises and subscription rates for consumers.

But Anthropic Direct may end up being something more. The filing doesn’t specifically say Direct compute could be rented to enterprise customers. Still, it’s a possibility; Anthropic could be building an AI-native cloud where enterprises could store their proprietary data and run Anthropic’s models in the same secure environment, potentially at a lower cost than building the same setup within an Amazon, Google, or Microsoft cloud.

That would give the Anthropic Direct brand name a very different meaning. Instead of accessing Claude models through a cloud provider they already use, customers would come directly to Anthropic. That could turn computing from a major overhead expense into a service Anthropic controls and rents to others for profit—a significant change to the company’s business model.

Some big obstacles stand in the way of such an ambition. Google, Amazon, and Microsoft are currently Anthropic’s largest compute suppliers, as well as the main distribution channels through which enterprises buy Claude. The S-1 notes that the three companies are at once Anthropic’s “investors, customers, distribution partners, and competitors.” If Anthropic challenged their cloud businesses directly, it would almost certainly strain those relationships. On the other hand, as more Direct data centers come online, Anthropic’s dependence on those cloud partners could decrease.

If the current rough parity among frontier models continues, the company that can deliver intelligence at the lowest overall cost per task—not per token—may have the edge. Anthropic’s filing suggests it is working toward that position on two fronts: getting more out of each chip and controlling more of the infrastructure those chips run on. Have retail investors factored that strategy into the price they’re willing to pay for Anthropic stock? The answer may emerge only after the stock has traded for a week or so.

California sues OpenAI over rogue AI agents

The California attorney general, Rob Bonta, sued OpenAI on Monday, alleging the company developed and tested advanced AI models without adequate safeguards. The suit centers on a July incident in which OpenAI agents escaped a testing environment and breached the systems of AI platform Hugging Face.

The complaint says OpenAI told the state it has lost control of its autonomous agents more than 80 times during testing. Bonta called the Hugging Face attack the “predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI” that puts growth ahead of safety. The state alleges violations of California’s unfair competition law and seeks an injunction, civil penalties, and disgorgement of profits. An OpenAI spokesperson said the suit “appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab.”

Jensen Huang says he’d be ‘honored’ to return as Nvidia CEO. Its board says nah

Nvidia’s board rejected the idea of reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO just hours after Huang said on Twitter that he’d be “honored” to return. On the company’s earnings call Tuesday afternoon, Harvey Jones, the board chair, said the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” The board had unanimously accepted Huang’s resignation. He has drawn support from Elon Musk, President Trump, and a petition with about 180,000 signatures, but the board is continuing its search for a permanent successor. Colette Kress, the CFO, is serving as interim CEO.

Huang broke his silence Tuesday, less than a week after resigning amid a personal conduct scandal and an investigation. In a statement on X, he said that if the board decides his return is in the best interest of shareholders, employees, the company, and America, “I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” Huang acknowledged making “serious mistakes in my personal life,” and said, “I own my mistakes completely.” He also said he is “committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation.” 

Demis Hassabis’s Isomorphic Labs raises $5 billion

Isomorphic Labs, the AI drug-discovery company founded and led by Demis Hassabis and spun out of Google DeepMind, announced a $5 billion Series C round of funding on Tuesday. Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital led the round, with participation from Andreessen Horowitz and other new investors and continued significant investment from Alphabet. Several existing backers—Thrive Capital, MGX, GV, CapitalG, Temasek, and the U.K. Sovereign AI Fund—also invested.

Isomorphic will use the money to scale IsoDDE, its drug-design engine built on AlphaFold-related technology, and to push drug candidates toward clinical trials. In a post on X, Hassabis said the company continues “to make rapid progress reimagining drug design from first principles with AI” to cut the time and cost of finding new medicines. No valuation was disclosed, but Bloomberg had reported the company was in talks to base the round on a valuation of about $50 billion.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] As widespread tech outages pile up, AI tools are in the spotlight again
items.content_html:
Inaccessible email inboxes. Banking delays. And a communications meltdown that grounded airplanes for hours, followed by waves of other travel disruptions.

In an increasingly interconnected world, some fear such disruptions could be the new normal.

Over the past week alone, problems that appeared to emerge from routine updates, security patches or other malfunctions surfaced at Microsoft, JP Morgan Chase and Apple, and even the U.S. government’s Federal Aviation Administration and National Security Agency. The Trump administration said there was “zero” indication the latest outages are linked, or caused by bad actors like cybercriminals.

The era of artificial intelligence has also raised the stakes for internet security overall. As AI tools uncover new vulnerabilities, many other companies and institutions are racing to patch them before they can be targeted by hackers, a cat-and-mouse game that can lead to a different set of glitches.

Social media platforms have been abuzz with a mixture of annoyance, confusion, conspiracy theories and jokes about the string of outages.

“To see several disruptions this close together, I think to a lot of people it’s made them realize how many parts of their lives they’ve handed over to these systems that we still, at this point, don’t fully understand,” Jake Smith, a content creator who regularly posts videos about politics on platforms like Instagram and YouTube, said in an interview. “I think it gives people a sense of helplessness to see all of it happening concurrently in a way.”

What’s gone offline recently

Outages and technology errors have piled up across sectors.

Late last week, a global Microsoft outage disrupted email and other workplace tools, plunging business and everyday services into disarray worldwide. Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot, were interrupted. Microsoft cited, in part, a failure during a recent upgrade to its servers, spanning from what the company later determined was a “latent defect” in a network fix it had begun deploying over the summer.

For air travel, a separate malfunction in the FAA’s network led to the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years on Friday. The stop lasted for more than four hours, and carriers cancelled and delayed swaths of flights as they worked to recover. Just days later, United Airlines saw its own system outage — forcing it to delay departing flights on Monday.

Online banking troubles also piled up on Monday. JPMorgan Chase said a software bug affected its internal hardware systems — causing transactional delays for its customers and others sending money to related accounts, sending jitters throughout the financial system before the problem was resolved.

And on Tuesday, Apple, Marriott and the NSA joined the growing list. Apple Music, the App Store and AppleCare services were temporarily disrupted after the company said an internal update caused outages. And Marriott said a technical issue also caused problems for sign-ins on its website and app.

Meanwhile, the NSA said an internal network it uses to communicate classified information was also offline Tuesday “during scheduled routine maintenance.”

The government — as well as Microsoft, United, JPMorgan Chase, Apple and Marriott — have again maintained there’s no evidence of these disruptions being linked or related to a cyberattack.

Microsoft also noted that its outage did not span from “AI / agents,” although it didn’t immediately specify the goal of the network fix it first deployed over the summer. Microsoft did not respond to an Associated Press request for further details, and the other companies did not provide additional comments Wednesday about their disruptions when contacted by the AP via email.

AI has helped identify vulnerabilities, but also adds to risks

AI has nonetheless come into the spotlight as experts evaluate these disruptions — both between heightened risks posed by the technology as well as its ability to detect security gaps.

For example, AI recently helped detect sweeping vulnerabilities for PHP, a general-purpose scripting language that powers websites around the world — leading to urgent calls for updates. And that security work has resulted in some limited outages and service delays.

President Donald Trump’s director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton, pointed directly to patching those security gaps when discussing the NSA’s outage this week. Clayton told Fox News that the patching following last month’s PHP alert has caused some systems to “not come back up” as expected. “That is what has happened at the NSA today,” he said.

Meanwhile, also this week, cybersecurity startup Calif said it used AI to help uncover a software bug in Java, one of the world’s most widely used programming languages and crucial for many big companies. Oracle, which owns Java, later released a security update and U.S. cyber authorities issued an advisory on Wednesday urging organizations to install it.

At the same time, others warn that the AI boom could open the door to additional disruptions.

“As AI adoption accelerates, we are likely to witness more incidents of this nature,” Raj Rajarajan, director of the Institute for Cyber Security at City St George’s, University of London, said last week.

He noted a lot of today’s digital infrastructure wasn’t originally designed to handle the “computational demands of large-scale AI services.”

While recent outages haven’t been tied to hackers or a coordinated attack, he and others also pointed to cybersecurity risks more broadly.

“AI is absolutely making it way easier for attackers to go and launch cyber attacks. It is not quite as good at creating patches for bugs, like fixing problems, as it is exploiting them,” said Justin Cappos, a cybersecurity professor at New York University’s Tandon School of Engineering.

In a cybersecurity report this week, Google said hackers and cyber criminals are “moving beyond basic prompting” and using increasingly sophisticated AI techniques to devise and carry out their attacks. The report, which focused on nefarious activity rather than outages, said techniques include using large language models and “agentic frameworks” to reverse engineering security patches to uncover vulnerabilities and exploit them.

Unraveling one (of just a few) major players in our online lives

Regardless, the latest outages offer yet more examples of the cascading effects that can erupt when a central player in tech, banking, travel or even the government runs into system errors that upend services.

Democratic Sen. Mark Warner, co-chair of the U.S. Senate’s Cybersecurity Caucus, acknowledged the widespread concern — and again stressed what this means in the AI era.

“These disruptions should serve as a wake-up call. It feels like every day brings another reminder that AI is moving faster than our ability to manage its consequences,” Warner said Tuesday. He also argued that the Trump administration hadn’t shown enough interest in confronting these challenges.

Still, “based on what we know today, there is good reason to believe these disruptions are the unintended consequences of efforts to make our systems safer,” Warner added.

—Wyatte Grantham-Philips, Kelvin Chan and Kaitlyn Huamani, AP Business Writers

items.title: [ft.com] UK tribunal orders disclosure of secret Apple data-access notice
items.content_html: The UK Investigatory Powers Tribunal ruled on Nov. 19 that the government could not keep secret a notice requiring Apple to give authorities access to encrypted customer data. The Home Office acknowledged issuing it. The judges rejected the claim that confirming the notice would harm national security, saying the government had not established that risk. The ruling addresses disclosure, not whether the government has the legal power to make the demand or what technical changes it requires. Those details remain secret, and a substantive hearing is expected in 2027. The dispute began with a January 2025 demand for access to users’ data worldwide, which Britain later withdrew after negotiations with the Trump administration. A second notice, issued in July 2026 and reportedly limited to UK customers, prompted Apple’s renewed challenge. Apple had already stopped offering its Advanced Data Protection encryption feature to new UK users in February 2025.

items.title: [MacRumors] UK Loses Secrecy Fight Over Apple 'Backdoor' Order
items.content_html:
Apple's challenge to a UK government demand for access to encrypted customer data can now be heard largely in public, after a tribunal rejected the Home Office's attempt to keep the order secret, according to the Financial Times.


The Investigatory Powers Tribunal today ruled that the British government had failed to demonstrate that confirming the demand would damage national security. The decision requires the Home Office to acknowledge that it served Apple with a technical capability notice (TCN), which is an order that can compel companies to make customer data accessible to UK security services, even when it is encrypted.

The government's position relied on its policy of neither confirming nor denying such notices. However, the tribunal found that disclosures to the media, including the Financial Times, and discussions with U.S. officials had already departed significantly from that policy.

In its judgment, the tribunal said the combined effect was that anyone following the dispute already knew Apple had received a TCN. It described the suggestion that official acknowledgment would threaten national security or give a malicious actor fresh information as "fanciful."

The ruling means that much of the legal action brought by Apple, alongside a separate challenge from Privacy International and Liberty, can proceed in open court.

Apple filed its latest legal challenge in July, following a second TCN. The Home Office had previously agreed to withdraw an earlier demand covering UK and U.S. customers after a dispute with the American government. The replacement notice is believed to focus on UK users specifically.

The dispute led Apple to stop offering Advanced Data Protection to new users in the UK in February 2025. The iCloud feature provides end-to-end encryption for additional categories of data, including device backups, photos, and notes, meaning Apple does not hold the keys needed to decrypt them.

UK users who had not already enabled ADP can no longer turn it on. Apple says it cannot switch the feature off on their behalf, so it can remain active on accounts where users previously enabled it and have not turned it off. The company said affected users will be given a period to disable ADP themselves to continue using ‌iCloud‌, but a deadline has still not been provided.

Without ADP, those additional categories of ‌iCloud‌ data use standard protection, under which Apple holds the encryption keys and can provide data in response to valid legal demands. iMessage and FaceTime remain end-to-end encrypted, as do categories protected by default, such as passwords and Health data.

The tribunal will now be able to hear much of the arguments over the government's encryption demands in public, with the legality of those demands still to be decided. Privacy International lists the substantive hearing for its separate challenge as scheduled for December 2026.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] ‘No one asked for this’: AI is being pushed on people—and they’re sick of it
items.content_html:
The AI era is fully here—and while companies bill it as a solution to problems, consequences like mass layoffs, environmental effects, privacy concerns, and the slopification of culture have many people fed up with something they never wanted in the first place.

The technology faces growing resentment from workers, who are being urged to embrace AI tools even as businesses have rushed to reduce their workforces in favor of automation. 

Online, many posts about AI capture a growing frustration with how these tools—and their disruptions—are being forced on users.

“Nobody asked for Google to be worse—but AI made it happen,” one X user recently remarked. “No one asked for computer hardware costs to rise—but AI made it happen. No one asked for human customer service to be replaced—but AI made it happen.”

In another post, Sarah Hoyt, a science fiction, fantasy, and mystery author, said she doesn’t hate artificial intelligence, but is “begging all the crazy people out there to stop pushing AI where no one asked for it.”

The disenchantment plays out in the data: In 2019, 81% of Glassdoor reviews mentioning AI were positive, the company said, compared with 43% this year. Meanwhile, Pew Research found that 52% of Americans were more concerned than excited about AI, up from 37% in 2021. And in an Ipsos poll from June, 67% of respondents thought AI would worsen the worker experience.

“The closest analog is the replacement of physical labor throughout the long Industrial Revolution,” said Jiemin Tina Wei, an assistant professor of history at Florida International University. But in this case, it’s “brain work,” rather than manual labor, that’s being replaced. 

“And now, the industries that are getting allegedly wiped out are the ‘low-hanging fruit’ of white-collar work,” she said.

But gutted livelihoods aren’t the only reason many are anti-AI.

The productivity paradox

Louis Hyman, a historian at Johns Hopkins University who specializes in labor and the American economy, points to a “productivity paradox”: a contradiction that was also generally true of the rise of computers in the ’80s, in which similarly dizzying investments didn’t necessarily make people better at their jobs as promised.

He points to snags like the frequency of software updates. “Every time you learn how to do something, suddenly they break it, and you have to relearn it.” With the introduction of AI, it’s “as if all software is being updated, all at once, everywhere.” Another part of the equation, he said, is that it isn’t clear how some people are using AI tools.

Hyman said he uses AI to write software and automate “boring tasks”—for example, he wrote a script to rotate the thousands of photos he takes of historical documents during archive visits so they all face right-side-up. But, he said, “most people are not wanting to sit down and write Python code to automate their job. They just want to do their job.” 

Added to that is the deep fear of being replaced once the work is automated. “I’m a tenured professor—I literally can’t be fired,” he said. “If I automate some boring part of my job, that just means I have more time to do the more interesting parts of my job. And that’s not true for all people, right?” 

A new occupational hazard

Another reason many people push back on AI is the lack of adequate guardrails—especially when it could cause major issues at work.

In one case, an AI tool deleted a software company’s entire database. In another, AI was blamed for deleting a fully edited season of a Swedish reality show mere weeks before the scheduled premiere. In medical settings, AI scribes have put inaccurate information in patient records, raising the question of who would be held liable for resulting medical errors. 

Meanwhile, misreads by AI identification tools used by law enforcement have led to wrongful arrests and injuries, per the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) AI Risk Initiative. Other AI-generated errors have popped up in court documents, federal reports, news stories, and fast-food drive-throughs. 

“The main point I’ve pushed and will continue to push [regarding] AI is ‘no one asked for this,’” radio host Adam Xii said on X, in response to news that Anthropic hallucinated details in its defense during a music copyright lawsuit. “So when a product or service no one asked for suddenly becomes ubiquitous, one must ask: why? Because AI tools are meant to generate more wealth for the wealthy at the expense of creatives.”

At the least, AI’s convenience is being offset by a need to check its work that has created new opportunities for human error. The proliferation of “workslop” even led a tech company’s CEO to fully ban AI use, as Inc. reported this summer. 

“A lot of what I’ve seen is kind of annoyance at the proselytizers at work—or the people who are heavy adopters—creating a lot of extra work for the people around them,” because those people downstream then have to check the work, Wei said.

Wei added that content moderation and data annotation work “can be extremely mentally taxing.” Research has found that “good” challenging work will be both difficult and interesting to certain extents, she said. But checking output is both difficult—because you have to look for every small potential error—and boring.

“You’re not producing knowledge, but merely supervising the production of words, knowledge, content,” Wei said.

The unwanted technological advances continue

AI’s intrusive nature—accompanied, again, by the threat of replacement—is reflected in workers’ behavior, not just in fed-up tweetstorms. One report found that nearly a third of workers surveyed, and 44% among Gen Z, had tried to sabotage their companies’ AI strategies.

Section, an AI planning and upskilling company, recently reported that 69% of workers surveyed said their organization had encouraged the use of AI agents, but only 16% actually used them. And 38% said they use other AI features.

The frustration hasn’t seemed to deter tech companies.

“We heard you wanted Copilot Mode at work,” read an X post from Microsoft that promoted Edge’s Copilot Mode for Business.

“No, you heard wrong,” a computer technician replied. “Literally no one asked for all this AI. In fact, everyone wants to know how to remove it.” 

Questions of organizations

In some cases, it seems companies are starting to discover that automation has some shortcomings.

In the U.S., 32% of hiring managers who eliminated positions in favor of AI have had to reinstate the same or similar roles, according to research from consulting firm Robert Half. Similarly, Gartner predicts that by 2027, half of companies that attributed reductions in staff to AI will rehire people to perform similar work.

Wei said the mismatch between the hopes for AI and the reality of its adoption relates to a quote from Bill Haywood, a famous labor organizer, who said that “the manager’s brains are under the workman’s cap.”

In other words, Wei said, “It’s really ultimately the workers who possess the knowledge and the know-how to run day-to-day operations. Some people have argued that the history of labor is just managers trying to take back that knowledge in an attempt to replace workers in the production.

“And I guess some people experience AI that way—that it’s being [imposed] upon them so that they train, ultimately, their final, automated replacement.”

Hyman said that a better alternative to the “adapt or die” mentality would be for organizations to use the technology to empower their employees. They should “actually say, ‘okay, we’re gonna create organizational conditions that let you replace yourself, and then focus on the work that needs to be done’—because the amount of work to be done is not finite, right?”

“I get told on a nearly weekly basis that historians are going to be replaced,” Hyman said. “So, yeah, it depends on how valuable you think getting reliable information and history is.”

He added that a world “where the only source of history or journalism is from either Open AI or Anthropic” would feel like an “Orwellian nightmare.”

“That seems not a great road to go down,” he said.

items.title: [cbsnews.com] Officials see AI-driven patching behind outages, not coordinated cyberattack
items.content_html: U.S. intelligence and law-enforcement officials told Congress they found no evidence that the recent service outages were coordinated cyberattacks, while lawmakers and security specialists warned that AI-assisted discovery of software flaws is driving rapid patching on systems not designed for that pace of change. Separately, attackers exploited a flaw in Optimizely’s website experimentation platform to inject malicious JavaScript onto sites associated with at least 178 organizations. Optimizely said it patched the flaw and removed the code, and officials have not linked that incident to the outages. Attackers are also using AI tools to locate weaknesses and speed up intrusions. The FBI warned that an AI tool called ARTEX helped hackers gain some privileged access to organizations in less than three hours, while Google reported seeing hackers use AI agents to find vulnerabilities and automate attacks. The National Security Agency’s classified internal network experienced intermittent service disruptions, prompting staggered staff arrivals while employees used alternative channels. An agency source said classified national-security work continued. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer called for a dedicated intelligence red team to examine whether the outages were connected and report to Congress by Dec. 1. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the administration would contact industry about sharing information on major patches before they take effect.

items.title: [gizmodo.com] AI-driven flaw discovery strains patching as outages hit US services
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

AI tools are rapidly uncovering software vulnerabilities and helping automate cyberattacks as outages disrupt U.S. email, flight operations, banking services and an internal National Security Agency communications network. Cybersecurity experts have linked some disruptions to rushed fixes for newly found flaws, but Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said the incidents were separate operational problems and officials had no indication of malicious activity or a coordinated attack. Hackers are also using AI to automate attacks. The FBI said hackers used the Artex AI framework in attacks worldwide, with some gaining privileged access in under three hours, while Palo Alto Networks linked another framework, Cairn, to 25 operations against at least 19 organizations. Researchers also used AI to find Java4Shell, a flaw in Java’s Base64 decoding library that could let an attacker execute commands on a vulnerable server. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency urged organizations to patch it. U.S. regulators sent inquiries to banks affected by outages, and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency plans a deeper review of the incidents. Canonical, the company behind Ubuntu, is separately offering AI-generated fixes to Ubuntu Pro customers through an optional early-release channel before its engineers complete normal review and testing.

items.title: [eff.org] US communities split over police license-plate cameras and privacy rules
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Communities across the United States are taking different approaches to police automated license-plate reader (ALPR) networks: voters in York, Maine, and League City, Texas, rejected their use, while Cedar Rapids approved a nearly $500,000 switch from Flock Safety to Axon without increasing its network of 70 cameras. Springfield, Massachusetts, has not advanced a proposed ban; councilors plan to review possible safeguards before deciding whether to send it forward. The systems record plates, timestamps and locations. Police say they can help investigate crimes and find missing people, while privacy advocates warn about tracking, misuse and data sharing beyond local jurisdictions. Suffolk County’s sheriff’s office has data-sharing relationships with slightly more than 400 agencies, established through system settings rather than formal written agreements. Ohio lawmakers are considering House Bill 725, which would set statewide rules for police use of plate data and make misuse a fifth-degree felony. The ACLU of Ohio argues the bill regulates data only after collection and could reduce public access to search information. Springfield’s committee plans to meet again after consulting the city’s Law Department.

items.title: [calif.io] AI-assisted research finds Java flaw enabling tailored server takeovers
items.content_html: The Java4Shell flaw disclosed by research firm Calif can corrupt memory in OpenJDK’s Base64 decoder and, in specific environments, let an unauthenticated attacker execute code remotely. The vulnerable code uses optimized assembly instructions on some x86-64 processors with AVX-512 VBMI; ARM64 systems do not use that code. Oracle released fixes on Nov. 17, and the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency urged organizations to patch immediately. A malformed Base64 string—64 “A” characters followed by “=”—can trigger the corruption, but it is not a universal exploit: an attacker must find a way to feed the input into a specific application and turn the overwrite into code execution. Calif demonstrated unauthenticated code execution in several widely used enterprise products, while other tested applications required a valid account. Calif researcher Quang Luong found the bug with AI coding assistance in about an hour and built an initial exploit in two more hours, at a reported cost of less than $200 for AI use. At the time of the reports, researchers and Canadian authorities had not confirmed exploitation in the wild. CISA advises organizations to inventory Java runtimes, including versions bundled with applications and containers, and prioritize internet-facing systems.

items.title: [theregister.com] Web-testing platform Optimizely breach exposes visitors at 178 sites to malware
items.content_html: Hackers exploited a vulnerability in website-testing platform Optimizely on Nov. 16, injecting malicious JavaScript into scripts used by 178 organizations, including the BBC, CNN, Zoom, IKEA, HSBC and Salesforce. Security researcher Scott Helme and cybersecurity firm Report URI found that the code reached visitors through Optimizely’s trusted delivery infrastructure, without requiring attackers to break into each customer’s servers. The scripts attempted to replace cryptocurrency wallet addresses, capture card details entered into website forms, steal browser cookies, take screenshots and load exploit kits targeting older Apple iPhones and iPads. Report URI tracked about $7,040 in cryptocurrency sent to attacker-linked wallets in roughly nine hours. Researchers could not establish how many card details were stolen and reported no confirmed iPhone takeover in this campaign. Optimizely said it patched the flaw, removed the injected code, revoked tokens and reset access for affected accounts. Salesforce disabled the scripts while investigating, and IKEA opened an inquiry. Equifax stopped using the service and said it found no evidence its systems were compromised.

items.title: [techxplore.com] Baidu chief warns AI adoption is failing to deliver business returns
items.content_html: Baidu Chief Executive Robin Li said at an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) business summit in Shenzhen on Nov. 17 that AI adoption in business is falling short of expectations. Despite rapid increases in computing and cloud spending and token use, many companies have not seen clear gains in revenue or profit, he said. He warned that failure to find effective applications could turn the AI boom into a bubble. Microsoft Chief Executive Satya Nadella raised a separate concern at a Microsoft Ignite roundtable in San Francisco. He said AI’s economic and political effects will depend on whether its benefits spread widely, warning that a single model could expand into health care, financial services and government. Li said companies need to identify real-world uses and adapt how they work to benefit from AI. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping were expected to discuss AI safety at APEC talks on Thursday, Nov. 19.

He said AI’s use in user-facing applications has lagged heavy spending on infrastructure and model development, and that most businesses using the technology have not seen higher revenue or profits. Investors are questioning whether revenue can justify planned spending on data centers and computing: AI providers are projected to spend $7 trillion on infrastructure through 2030, while Gartner forecasts at most $3.6 trillion in related revenue over that period. US stocks fell on Monday, with the S&P 500 down 1.9% and the Nasdaq Composite down 2.5%. Baidu has reported six consecutive quarterly revenue declines, which Li attributed in part to difficulties in online marketing.

items.content_html: Apple’s second developer beta of macOS 27.3 adds more targeted permission choices and stronger warnings for apps seeking broad access to Mac files or control over other apps, following writer Jason Aten’s September claim that Meta’s Muse AI agent read his messages. Apple says Full Disk Access can expose messages, email, photos, videos and data from other accounts, allowing an app to read, change, delete and export files. Meta Superintelligence Labs executive David Singleton countered that Muse can read message content on a Mac only if users grant it Full Disk Access and enable the Messages connector. Apple’s changes do not revoke permissions users previously approved, so existing access remains active unless users change or remove it in Privacy & Security settings. The controls are in developer beta 2; Apple has not announced a public release date.

items.title: [reuters.com] US rule puts overseas AI compute hubs under licensing scrutiny
items.content_html: The new U.S. controls subject large overseas AI-computing operations and chip supply chains to additional licensing scrutiny. Malaysia’s YTL Power, an Nvidia infrastructure partner, fell nearly 10% on Tuesday, while data-center-linked companies across Southeast Asia also declined. Analysts warned that operators dependent on Chinese AI customers could face longer licensing and customer-verification processes. Malaysia has approved 385.7 billion ringgit ($95 billion) in data-center-related investments since 2021, and Thailand’s data centers represent about 3,400 megawatts of IT load. The Commerce Department’s interim rule, issued Nov. 16, targets remote access to advanced U.S. chips through overseas data centers, closing a route Chinese AI developers had used to rent computing capacity rather than import restricted chips. It applies to data centers providing more than 12 million total processing performance (TPP) to covered customers; the measure counts linked facilities together and requires checks on direct and indirect ownership. Existing operators have 90 days after the rule takes effect to seek licenses, while commercial recommendation systems are exempt. Singapore said it is consulting affected firms and U.S. authorities about implementation and how local businesses can retain “trusted access” to advanced chips. The rules also formally rescind the Biden administration’s 2025 AI Diffusion framework, which Trump officials had said they would not enforce.

At a Senate committee hearing, the company argued the proposed lawful-access law could require providers to build surveillance capabilities or comply with confidential orders, putting encrypted data at risk. Meta’s director of privacy and public policy, Robyn Greene, said it was not technically possible to comply while continuing to offer secure end-to-end encryption. The Senate is reviewing the bill after Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree amended it to limit when companies could be required to decrypt information. The government says the legislation gives police and intelligence agencies tools to prevent and investigate modern crime, while Meta and other technology companies say the changes leave security gaps. Meta’s Rachel Curran said the company would review its options if the bill became law without further changes.

items.title: [MacRumors] macOS 27.3 Warns Against Giving AI Apps Full Mac Control
items.content_html:
With the latest macOS 27.3 beta, Apple is giving Mac users more control over the data they share and the access they give to apps, including apps that use AI agents. Apple today informed developers about upcoming changes to the Full Disk Access API and the Device Control and Data Access API.


Here's what Apple says is changing:

  • The current Device Control and Data Access setting will be split into two options that make it clearer to users what they're permitting. The setting is becoming System & App Protection Override and Accessibility.

  • There will be a single method for granting permissions by selecting the app requesting access from a list.

  • Apple will encourage users to grant access to just the specific apps (in System & App Protection Override) or folders (for Full Disk Access) required for workflows.

  • Apple will better inform users about the data apps will receive access to or control over if full permissions are given.

  • Users will have an option to configure apps to ask each time for required access rather than granting an app unrestricted access.

  • There will be a transparency indicator when a requesting app is controlling another app with System & App Protection Override. The indicator will be displayed in the Mac menu bar.


Apple says developers will need to adjust user onboarding and make sure apps can "gracefully handle" access to a limited set of folders or apps when using the APIs being overhauled.


Apps that use Full Disk Access for disk backup or the new Accessibility settings for assistive technologies can request entitlements to offer the same experience for new installations that they offered before macOS 27.3.

Right now, known apps keep their current experience without an entitlement, and app permissions granted by users prior to macOS 27.3 will remain in effect. Mac users will see these changes when approving new app permission requests, and entitlement details are coming soon.

Last month, Apple said it would add "additional controls" for Full Disk Access on Macs because of the risks posed by AI agents. Apple warned that some developers are using Full Disk Access in ways that can put users at risk, exposing files, mail, messages, browsing history, and more.
This article, "macOS 27.3 Warns Against Giving AI Apps Full Mac Control" first appeared on MacRumors.com

items.title: [zdnet.com] AI agents expand cyber risks as companies struggle to enforce controls
items.content_html: Security experts warn that increasingly autonomous AI agents can move across company systems at machine speed, complicating conventional identity and access controls. Agents may query databases, call application programming interfaces, use tools or act through an employee’s account. Experts say a login record alone may not show who initiated an action or what the agent did. European Central Bank Vice-President Boris Vujčić said AI is increasing the scale and speed of cyberattacks, while banks face delays in adapting their defenses. Weill Cornell Medicine said an employee entered patient information into AI tools during a research study without authorization. A DNSFilter survey found that half of healthcare security leaders confirmed or suspected that employees had connected unapproved AI tools to critical systems. A Linux Foundation survey of 308 cybersecurity practitioners found that 58% said development teams release code faster than security staff can review it. Security specialists recommend giving each agent a distinct identity, limiting its permissions to a specific task, setting credentials to expire and recording actions for review. The Electronic Frontier Foundation, a digital-rights group, says established security practices could have prevented the OpenAI–Hugging Face incident and similar incidents. It calls for enforceable standards, independent investigations and notice to affected parties after incidents.

items.title: [openai.com] OpenAI signs agreements with four outside groups to assess AI safety risks
items.content_html: OpenAI signed agreements on Nov. 16 with four outside groups — Apollo Research, METR, Transluce and Goodfire — to conduct embedded assessments of its AI models and safeguards. Apollo’s six evaluators will examine whether models try to undermine safety controls for themselves or successor models, including during training and internal use. The other groups will assess model internals, unintended behavior, monitoring and post-training safety tests. The assessments extend beyond the usual practice of testing models after training and shortly before release. Goodfire will study model internals and training runs, METR will test for harmful behavior and whether monitoring catches it, and Transluce will review post-training evaluations. OpenAI and Transluce plan a roughly eight-week follow-up in early 2027 to examine how test results inform release decisions. Apollo’s access is limited to agreed models, claims and time periods. OpenAI can withhold some information for security, technical or intellectual-property reasons and may restrict the evidence published alongside findings.

items.title: [news18.com] US-led group signs pact to secure AI supply chains from China
items.content_html: The United States and eight partners signed the San Francisco Declaration on the Secure Foundations of Enduring Prosperity, pledging to identify and protect artificial-intelligence technologies and supply chains viewed as vulnerable to China’s influence. Japan, Australia, Israel, the United Kingdom, South Korea, India, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates joined the United States; Germany, Sweden, the Netherlands and the European Commission are expected to sign next week. The agreement is part of the US-led Pax Silica initiative and covers supply-chain risks involving semiconductors, critical minerals, energy infrastructure and other AI-related systems. Its signatories plan to form working groups to identify vulnerabilities, share information and explore investment hubs. US economic affairs official Jacob Helberg said AI supply chains cross borders, making their security a shared responsibility.
